extracted.intended_audience: elementary-school teachers, school inspectors, and education policymakers (readers of scientific and educational periodicals)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and evaluative criteria for what elementary education should include (particularly elementary science/knowledge of common things), how it should be taught, and what pedagogical aims it should pursue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of elementary science (elementary knowledge of common things)
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of elementary science, or 'elementary knowledge of common things', should be included among subjects for which grants are given under the education code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simpler phrase 'elementary knowledge' to avoid frightening ministers, inspectors, school boards, and teachers; the nation urgently needs these basic scientific understandings in elementary schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education aims — cultivate intelligence and impart applicable knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The ends of education are twofold — first, to cultivate the intelligence to facilitate the acquirement and application of knowledge; and secondly, to impart the knowledge which has to be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula and teaching practices should be judged by whether they serve these two ends, avoiding omission of useful subjects or inclusion of irrelevant ones that do not promote these ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rote memorization / higher-centre engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Common processes of teaching often appeal to lower centres which govern memory of sounds rather than to higher ones which are organs of ratiocination and volition; much which passes for education is a degradation to efforts below natural capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid book-work that demands only sequence-memory of sounds; ensure pupils understand meanings and engage higher intellectual faculties so that learning persists beyond vacations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of object lessons and experimental illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Object lessons, where pupils are exercised about things instead of words, are highly valuable; teaching something about gravitation, atmospheric pressure, effects of temperature, etc., which admit experimental illustration, are steps toward real mental development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage pupils to make statements in their own words; object lessons increase capacity to acquire and retain new facts and are preferable to purely verbal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include drawing to teach accurate observation
rubrics_metrics.description: In elementary schools give an important place to the art of drawing, which teaches accurate observation of the forms of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing trains observation and complements scientific object lessons; it has practical consequences for pupils' future skill and employability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach with reference to child's home and surroundings
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise teacher's efforts should be guided with reference to the position and surroundings of a child at home, and should seek to supplement deficiencies of home training and example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt instruction to pupils' backgrounds; among the poor an explanation of physical causes of common events can be revelatory and open paths to improved practical skill and social mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach practical, everyday physical causes and natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach physical causes of common events (e.g., why water rises in a pump), elements of natural science, and simple matters that pupils meet daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such instruction will render pupils more skillful workers and may lead some to better positions; it provides practical utility and national benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impart knowledge about conduct, industry, and social consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Every schoolmaster should make pupils understand how production (industry) leads to wealth and how destruction (idleness) leads to poverty; why confidence and honesty are necessary to enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and practical instruction concerning conduct and its influence on life should be enforced by precept and illustrated by example; widespread teaching of these matters would help social-economic relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'education' from mere 'instruction'
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and instruction are different; one may learn many 'facts' at school yet have true education begin only after leaving it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and teaching should aim to produce real mental development, not just accumulation of factual knowledge; reformers should emphasize formative, not merely informational, goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science-teaching is accessible and pleasant for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Science-teaching has been found comparatively easy and pleasant by children (e.g., in Scotch schools), contrary to fears that it would be difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments against introducing elementary science on grounds of difficulty are unfounded; science can relieve dull routine and engage pupils effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid curriculum decisions based solely on inspector convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition that adoption of elementary science would entail temporary uncertainty about inspection subjects applies only if schools exist for inspectors' convenience; such an objection should not determine curriculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum choices should be driven by educational ends and national benefit, not by administrative convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment accountability — avoid wasting public funds on irrelevant subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The nation spends large and increasing sums on schools; it's urgent these sums not be misapplied by omitting useful subjects or including others with no tendency to promote educational ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy must ensure funds support subjects that cultivate intelligence and impart applicable knowledge, e.g., elementary science and practical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/chemical explanation for biological motility (avoid vitalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motility (in monera) consists of alternate expansion and contraction of protoplasm caused by processes of chemical composition (expansion) and decomposition (contraction); there is no need to appeal to a specific vital force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations of life should seek direct chemical evidence (products separated and eliminated, combining substances uniting under observation) rather than invoke 'qualitas occulta' or metaphysical vital forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mechanism and molecular chemistry to invoking new forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The contraction and extension seen in living matter are physical concomitants of definite chemical occurrences; vital processes are displays of specific chemistry inherent in substances, not transferences of mysterious agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should attempt to link organic phenomena to known molecular forces and recognize that specific molecular constitution determines behavior (analogy to H2O expansibility vs protoplasm's greater synthetical wealth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative observation of simple organisms to infer general principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Monera give plain information: by observing them one can ascertain whether motility is due to chemical composition/decomposition; these simple organisms allow direct witnessing of expansion/contraction and accompanying chemical changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful, visible observation of simple life-forms and their accompanying chemical transformations provides legitimate grounds for inferring general principles about life and refuting vitalism.
